questions.why: $1\cdot2 + 2\cdot0 + 2\cdot(-1) = 0$. A zero dot product between non-zero vectors means they are perpendicular.

questions.q: What is the cosine similarity of $x$ and $3x$ for any non-zero $x$?
questions.why: Cosine similarity divides out both lengths, so scaling a vector by a positive constant leaves it unchanged. Scaling by a negative constant gives $-1$.

questions.q: Why compute $\|x\|_p$ as $m\,\big(\sum_i |x_i/m|^p\big)^{1/p}$ with $m = \max_i |x_i|$?
options: It is the definition of the $p$-norm
It avoids overflow (or underflow) when raising large or tiny values to the power $p$
questions.why: For $x_i = 10^{200}$ and $p = 2$, $x_i^2$ overflows. Dividing by the largest magnitude keeps every term in $[0, 1]$ and gives the same value after rescaling.

questions.q: As $p \to \infty$, $\|x\|_p$ approaches what?
questions.why: The largest component dominates the sum as $p$ grows, so the norm tends to the max norm.

questions.q: For pairwise Euclidean distances between rows of $A$ `(m, d)` and $B$ `(n, d)`, the identity $\|a - b\|^2 = \|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2 - 2a\cdot b$ is used because...
options: It turns the work into one matrix product $AB^\top$ without an $(m, n, d)$ intermediate
It works only for unit vectors
It is more accurate than subtracting directly
questions.why: The expansion replaces the broadcast difference with a BLAS matmul. It can produce tiny negative values from cancellation, so clip at 0 before the square root.

questions.q: The outer product of $u \in \mathbb R^3$ and $v \in \mathbb R^4$ has what shape and rank?
questions.why: Every column of $uv^\top$ is a multiple of $u$, so the matrix has rank 1. Sums of outer products build higher-rank matrices, as in the SVD.

questions.q: Can $(1, 1)$ be written as a linear combination of $(1, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$?
options: Yes, any two vectors span $\mathbb R^2$
No, both vectors lie on the x-axis, so they only span that line
questions.why: The two vectors are linearly dependent and span only the x-axis, so no combination has a non-zero second component.

questions.q: In attention, scores are $q\cdot k/\sqrt d$. Why divide by $\sqrt d$?
options: To make the softmax sum to 1
To normalise $q$ and $k$ to unit length
For random unit-variance components the dot product's variance grows like $d$; dividing keeps it near 1
questions.why: A sum of $d$ independent products has variance $d$. Unscaled scores would saturate the softmax for large $d$, giving tiny gradients.

questions.q: $A$ is $2\times3$ and $B$ is $3\times4$. What is the shape of $AB$, and is $BA$ defined?
questions.why: Inner dimensions must match: $(2\times3)(3\times4) = 2\times4$. For $BA$ the inner dimensions are 4 and 2, so it isn't defined.

questions.q: How can you compute $\mathrm{tr}(AB)$ for $n\times n$ matrices without forming $AB$?
questions.why: $\mathrm{tr}(AB) = \sum_{i,j} A_{ij}B_{ji}$, the elementwise product of $A$ and $B^\top$, summed. The trace of a product isn't the product of traces.

questions.q: Which property holds for all conformable matrices?
questions.why: Transposing reverses the order of a product. Matrix multiplication isn't commutative, and the determinant isn't additive.

questions.q: What is $\det\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 4 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, and what does it tell you?
questions.why: $2\cdot2 - 1\cdot4 = 0$. The second row is twice the first, so the rows are dependent and the matrix has no inverse.

questions.q: Cofactor expansion computes an $n\times n$ determinant in how many operations, roughly?
options: $O(n!)$, which is why libraries use LU instead ($O(n^3)$)
questions.why: Each level of expansion creates $n$ subproblems of size $n - 1$. LU factorisation gives the determinant as the product of the pivots.

questions.q: You compute the rank of a nearly singular matrix with `np.linalg.matrix_rank`. What does it actually count?
options: Singular values above a tolerance based on the largest singular value and machine precision
questions.why: Floating-point matrices are rarely exactly singular. Rank is defined numerically by thresholding the singular values, typically at $\sigma_{max}\cdot\max(m, n)\cdot\epsilon$.

questions.q: The Hadamard product $A\odot B$ requires what?
options: The columns of $A$ match the rows of $B$
questions.why: It multiplies matching entries, so shapes must be identical (NumPy would broadcast, but the strict definition doesn't).

questions.q: Computing $Ax$ for an $m\times n$ matrix needs how many multiplications?
questions.why: Each of the $m$ outputs is a dot product of length $n$. A naive $n\times n$ matrix product needs $n^3$.

questions.q: Projecting $b = (3, 4)$ onto the direction $a = (1, 0)$ gives what?
questions.why: $\mathrm{proj}_a b = \frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a}a = 3\cdot(1, 0)$. The residual $(0, 4)$ is orthogonal to $a$.

questions.q: Why is modified Gram-Schmidt preferred over classical Gram-Schmidt?
options: It works on non-square matrices only
It loses less orthogonality to rounding errors
questions.why: Both produce the same result in exact arithmetic. Modified Gram-Schmidt subtracts projections one at a time against the updated vector, so errors don't compound as quickly.

questions.q: During Gram-Schmidt, a new vector's residual norm is nearly 0. What does that mean?
options: The vector is orthogonal to the previous ones
The vector is (nearly) a linear combination of the previous ones, so the rank is deficient
questions.why: A tiny residual means almost nothing new is left after removing the existing directions, so it shouldn't become a new basis vector.

questions.q: You need to solve $Ax = b$. Why avoid computing `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`?
options: The two give different answers in exact arithmetic
A direct solve is faster and more accurate
questions.why: `np.linalg.solve` factorises $A$ once and back-substitutes; forming the inverse costs more and amplifies rounding error.

questions.q: Why does LU decomposition use partial pivoting?
options: To avoid dividing by zero or tiny pivots, which blow up rounding errors
questions.why: Swapping rows so the largest available entry is the pivot keeps multipliers at most 1 in magnitude. Without it, $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ can't be factorised at all.

questions.q: A square system $Ax = b$ has $\det A = 0$. Which is true?
options: It has either no solution or infinitely many
It always has infinitely many solutions
questions.why: A singular $A$ maps $\mathbb R^n$ onto a lower-dimensional subspace. If $b$ is in that subspace there are infinitely many solutions; otherwise none.

questions.q: $Q$ has orthonormal columns. What is $Q^\top Q$?
questions.why: Entry $(i, j)$ of $Q^\top Q$ is $q_i\cdot q_j$, which is 1 on the diagonal and 0 off it. $QQ^\top$ is the identity only when $Q$ is square.

questions.q: Least squares $\min\|Ax - b\|$ with $A$ of full column rank has the solution...
options: $x = (A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top b$, best computed via QR
questions.why: The normal equations give that formula, but forming $A^\top A$ squares the condition number. Solving with QR ($Rx = Q^\top b$) avoids it.

questions.q: In $A = U\Sigma V^\top$, what does keeping the top $k$ singular values give?
options: The best rank-$k$ approximation in both the spectral and Frobenius norms
questions.why: The Eckart-Young theorem says truncated SVD is optimal. The Frobenius error is $\sqrt{\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2}$.

questions.q: For a symmetric matrix $A = Q\Lambda Q^\top$, how do you compute $A^{10}$ cheaply?
questions.why: The $Q^\top Q$ pairs in the middle cancel, so powers act only on the eigenvalues.

questions.q: Which matrices have a Cholesky factorisation $A = LL^\top$?
questions.why: Cholesky needs symmetry and positive pivots. A failed Cholesky is a cheap test that a matrix (such as a covariance) isn't positive definite.

questions.q: Given a Cholesky factor $L$ of $A$, what is $\log\det A$?
questions.why: $\det A = (\det L)^2 = \prod_i L_{ii}^2$. Summing logs avoids the overflow that the product would cause for large matrices.

questions.q: The projection matrix onto the column space of $A$ (full column rank) is $P = A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$. What is $P^2$?
questions.why: Projecting twice is the same as projecting once, so $P$ is idempotent. It is also symmetric for orthogonal projections.

questions.q: Householder QR is preferred to Gram-Schmidt for which reason?
options: It is the only method that works for square matrices
It produces a $Q$ that stays orthogonal to machine precision
questions.why: Each Householder reflection is exactly orthogonal, so errors don't erode orthogonality the way successive projections can.

questions.q: For an underdetermined system with infinitely many solutions, what does $x = A^+ b$ return?
options: The first solution found by elimination
The solution with the smallest Euclidean norm
The solution with the most zeros
questions.why: The pseudoinverse picks the solution lying in the row space of $A$, which is orthogonal to the null space and therefore shortest.

questions.q: What are the singular values of an orthogonal matrix?
questions.why: An orthogonal matrix preserves lengths, so it stretches nothing: $Q^\top Q = I$ means every singular value is 1.

questions.q: Why use the Mahalanobis distance instead of Euclidean distance for outlier scoring?
options: It ignores outliers in the covariance estimate
It accounts for feature scales and correlations through the covariance
questions.why: $\sqrt{(x - \mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu)}$ measures distance in units of the data's spread in each direction, so a point far along a low-variance direction stands out.

questions.q: PCA by SVD of the centred data $X = U\Sigma V^\top$ ($n$ rows). What fraction of variance does component $i$ explain?
questions.why: The covariance eigenvalues are $\sigma_i^2/(n - 1)$, and the constant cancels in the ratio. Using unsquared singular values is a common mistake.

questions.q: What happens if you forget to centre the data before PCA?
options: Nothing; PCA centres internally in every implementation
The first component tends to point towards the mean instead of the direction of largest variance
questions.why: SVD of uncentred data finds directions of largest second moment around the origin, which is dominated by the mean when it is large.

questions.q: Ridge regression adds $\lambda\|w\|^2$. What does that do to the normal equations?
options: $(X^\top X + \lambda I)w = X^\top y$, which is always invertible for $\lambda > 0$
It removes the need for $X^\top X$
questions.why: Adding $\lambda$ to every eigenvalue makes the matrix positive definite. The intercept is usually left unpenalised.

questions.q: ZCA whitening differs from PCA whitening how?
options: It rotates back to the original axes, so whitened data stays close to the input
It uses the correlation matrix instead of the covariance
questions.why: PCA whitening is $\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top x$; ZCA is $U\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top x$. Both give identity covariance, but ZCA keeps features aligned with the originals (useful for images).

questions.q: Kernel ridge regression with an RBF kernel solves $(K + \lambda I)\alpha = y$. What is the cost for $n$ training points?
questions.why: The kernel matrix is $n\times n$ regardless of the feature dimension. That cubic cost is why large-scale kernel methods use approximations.

questions.q: In multi-head attention with model width $D$ and $H$ heads, the per-head width is usually...
options: $D$, so each head is as wide as the model
$D/H$, so total compute matches one head of width $D$
questions.why: Splitting the projection into $H$ slices of width $D/H$ gives several attention patterns at the same parameter count as one full-width head.

questions.q: A causal attention mask sets scores above the diagonal to $-\infty$ before the softmax. What would setting them to 0 do?
options: Leak future tokens, because $e^0 = 1$ still gives them weight
questions.why: Only $-\infty$ (or a very negative number) gives zero weight after exponentiation. A score of 0 is an ordinary, often large, weight.
